Chapter 7: The Responsibility of the Intellectual—Choosing Sides
In the middle of all these new challenges, there's another kind of struggle happening—one that's quieter, but just as important. It plays out in classrooms, in the stories we read in the paper, and in those thoughtful, late-night conversations with friends.
The role of the intellectual, the writer, and the teacher really starts to matter here. They're the ones shaping how a country sees itself. They're the storytellers guiding us toward the kind of future we can imagine.
Picture a university lecturer. He was once known for his bold criticism of colonialism. But now, he's been asked by the new government to write speeches—ones that praise the new leaders and quietly ignore the country's real problems.
You can almost feel the pressure building—from his family, his students, even his own conscience. Should he speak the truth and risk losing his job? Or stay quiet, hoping things will somehow get better?
It's a crossroads that feels familiar to so many. People who once fought fiercely for freedom can find themselves tempted by comfort, or the lure of recognition. Suddenly, the intellectual class risks becoming a new elite—more focused on keeping their own status than on challenging injustice.
It becomes easy to slip into endless debates, high above the struggles of ordinary people. But here's the thing—honest voices are needed now more than ever. The stories we choose to tell, whether about our past or our dreams for the future, shape what people believe and what they're willing to do.
If intellectuals turn their backs on ordinary people, the distance between leaders and the rest of society just keeps growing. And that dream of a truly just society? It starts to feel out of reach.
But not everyone takes the easy path.
Imagine a poet, inspired by the strength she sees in her neighbors, writing verses that celebrate both their struggles and their hopes. Or a teacher, urging his students to ask tough questions—and to see themselves as people who can make real change.
These actions might seem small, but they matter. They plant seeds of possibility.
So, what’s the real responsibility of the intellectual? It’s not about standing above the people—it’s about standing with them. Listening, learning, and using your voice for justice and dignity.
It’s never easy. The risks are real. But without this commitment, the promise of liberation slips further away.
